cues.text: Put Nell exactly on Marshall's line. Exactly on it. The money coming in is precisely enough to cover everything, including the cost of her money.
Marshall says she should be indifferent. Build, or do not build. It makes no difference either way.
Hang on. There is a third thing she could do, and neither of those is it.
Give her one very simple plan. It is not even the best plan — it is just a plan, and it is enough to make the point.
Wait a fixed stretch of time. Then look at the money coming in. If it is above the line, build. If it is not, never build.
Now watch what the future might do, starting from that point. Here are five futures. Nobody knows which one happens.
Some of them end up high. Some end up low. That is what uncertainty looks like.
In the two futures that end up high, she looks, she sees the money is well above the line, and she builds. She gains.
In the two futures that end up low, she looks, and she does not build. She gains nothing.
But look at that again, because everything turns on it. She gains nothing — and she loses nothing.
So do the sum. Mix together some positive outcomes and some zeros, and weigh each by how likely it is.
The answer is bigger than nothing. It cannot be anything else.
Which means waiting beats acting, at the very point where the textbook says she should not care either way. So the textbook's line is in the wrong place.
Here is the sentence. Waiting lets her avoid the downside over that stretch of time, while keeping the upside.
That selective removal of risk — cutting off the bad half and keeping the good half — is what waiting is worth.
One more thing, and it is the most counter-intuitive part of the chapter, so I am going to say it twice.
This has nothing whatsoever to do with disliking risk.
Nell is assumed not to mind risk at all. She would take a fair gamble without blinking. And she still waits.
The trade she is making is between risk now and risk later. It is not about nerves. It is about timing.
start exactly on the textbook's line
good futures pay · bad ones cost nothing
gains + zeros > nothing
None of this is about disliking risk.
